### Lifetime

- All future AI tools & feature updates included

- Priority processing & early access to new releases

One-time payment, no auto-renewal. Secure checkout by Dodo Payments.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the difference between Pro and Lifetime plans?

Both plans give you the exact same full access to the complete SkillTa suite: AI Career Quiz, AI Resume Reviewer, Skill Gap Analyzer, 50+ Country Tech Ecosystem, and all 50+ roadmaps with PDF export, plus an ad-free, clean experience. Guests and users without an active plan may see ads. The only difference is duration: Pro gives 1 full year ($3) while Lifetime gives permanent access forever ($10) with all future updates.

### Is this a subscription or a one-time payment?

Both Pro ($3) and Lifetime ($10) are 100% one-time payments. There are no hidden fees, no auto-debit renewals, and no surprise charges. When your Pro year ends, you choose whether to renew.

### How long does the career quiz take?

The AI Career Quiz takes approximately 5-10 minutes. It includes 10 smart questions designed to understand your interests, skills, and career goals. Unlock full results with a Pro or Lifetime plan.

### Can I retake the quiz if my interests change?

Absolutely! You can retake the quiz anytime. If you're signed in, all your quiz results are saved to your dashboard so you can compare different paths and track your career journey over time.

### Are the learning roadmaps included?

Roadmaps are included in your SkillTa Pro or Lifetime access. We provide high-quality, ad-free guidance for a one-time low cost, ensuring you get the most accurate and updated career paths without the noise of ads.

### How accurate is the AI recommendation?

Our AI is trained on data from 10,000+ tech professionals and uses machine learning to match your profile with career paths. It has a 92% accuracy rate in recommending suitable tech careers, but it's one tool among many. Always combine it with mentorship and personal research.

### Can I download my roadmap as PDF?

Yes! Once you get your personalized roadmap, you can download it as a PDF with all the learning resources, project ideas, and timeline included. Perfect for offline reading or sharing with mentors.

### Do I need prior tech experience to use SkillTa?

No, SkillTa is designed for everyone—from complete beginners to career switchers with some background. The quiz adapts to your current level and recommends learning paths accordingly. Many users are transitioning from non-tech fields.

### How often are the roadmaps updated?

We update our roadmaps every quarter to reflect the latest industry trends, tools, and market demands. Your saved roadmaps automatically stay current so you're always following best practices.

### Can I save my progress if I'm not signed in?

Quiz results can be viewed immediately, but they won't persist if you close your browser without signing in. Sign in with Google to save everything and access your dashboard anytime. It's a one-click setup!

# About SkillTa — AI Career Guidance for Tech

> SkillTa helps aspiring tech professionals find their ideal career path with honest, data-driven AI guidance. Career quiz, 50+ roadmaps, salary insights, and personalized recommendations for students, freshers & career switchers.

Canonical: https://www.skillta.tech/about

# About SkillTa

We believe everyone deserves clarity about their career path. SkillTa uses AI to match your unique traits with the perfect tech career.

## Our Mission

Help aspiring tech professionals find their ideal career path with honest, data-driven guidance — not hype.

## How It Works

Our AI analyzes your interests, skills, and personality across 10 carefully crafted questions to find your best match.

## Why We Built This

Too many people waste time on the wrong career path. We want to save you months of confusion with clear, actionable roadmaps.

## What's Next

We're building AI mentoring, progress tracking, community features, and premium roadmaps. Stay tuned for updates.

## Built with ❤️ for the tech community

SkillTa is free to use and always will be for core features. Our goal is to make quality career guidance accessible to everyone, regardless of background. Our goal is to make quality career guidance accessible to everyone, regardless of background.

# The SkillTa Story

> Why SkillTa was built and how plan purchases and guest advertising support the platform.

Canonical: https://www.skillta.tech/story

# The SkillTa Story

Why we built an honest AI career platform — and how your support helps us keep building.

## Where it started

SkillTa started with a simple frustration: thousands of students in India and around the world spend years choosing a tech career based on YouTube hype, random Reddit threads, or whatever their friends picked. There was no honest, personalized guide — just noise, coaching ads, and "top 10 careers" listicles. We wanted to build the tool we wished we had when we were 17: an AI that actually listens, understands your strengths, and gives you a real roadmap — not a sales pitch.

## Our mission

SkillTa exists to make career guidance **honest and high-quality** for students. Our Pro and Lifetime plans include the Career Suite and an ad-free, clean experience. Guests and users without an active plan may see advertisements, helping support the platform.

## The hard truth about running SkillTa

Building SkillTa costs real money every single day. Here's where it goes:

- **AI API bills** — every quiz result you get is generated by an AI model that charges us per request.

- **Domain & hosting** — skillta.tech, server bills, database, and email delivery are ongoing costs.

- **Marketing** — reaching students who need this the most costs money we don't have yet.

- **Development time** — hours of coding, designing, and testing every feature.

## Why we're asking for your help

Plan purchases, guest advertising, and optional donations help cover the ongoing costs of SkillTa. Active Pro and Lifetime users always receive an **ad-free, clean experience**. A donation supports development; it is separate from purchasing a plan.

Every contribution on Ko-fi helps fund AI usage, hosting, and improvements to our career tools. Thank you for supporting an independent project.

## What your donation unlocks (for everyone)

- Continued development of a focused career platform with ad-free Pro and Lifetime access.

- Better AI models for more accurate career matches.

- More career roadmaps, blog guides, and comparison tools.

- Subsidized access for students in need through our mission fund.

- A small indie project that stays independent — not owned by an ed-tech giant.

If SkillTa helped you find your path, please consider chipping in. Every donation, no matter how small, helps us keep building the best career tools.

Thank you for being part of the SkillTa story. 💜

# Frontend Developer Roadmap

> Craft beautiful, interactive user experiences

Canonical: https://www.skillta.tech/roadmaps/frontend-developer

Frontend developers bring designs to life. You'll build the visual and interactive parts of websites and apps that users directly interact with.

## Key facts

| Metric | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Difficulty | Moderate |
| Time to job-ready | 6-12 months to job-ready |
| Demand | Very High |
| Salary (India) | ₹4-15 LPA (entry) → ₹15-40 LPA (senior) |
| Salary (Global) | $50K-80K (entry) → $120K-200K+ (senior) |
| Growth | Excellent — every company needs frontend developers. Growing demand for React/Next.js specialists. |

## Required skills

- HTML/CSS
- JavaScript
- React/Vue/Angular
- TypeScript
- Responsive Design
- Git
- UI/UX Principles

## Learning roadmap

### Phase 1: Fundamentals (1-2 months)

- **HTML5** — Semantic markup, accessibility, forms
- **CSS3** — Flexbox, Grid, animations, responsive design
- **JavaScript Basics** — Variables, functions, DOM manipulation, events

Resources:

- MDN Web Docs
- freeCodeCamp
- The Odin Project

Projects:

- Personal portfolio website
- Responsive landing page
- Interactive form

### Phase 2: Core Skills (2-3 months)

- **Advanced JavaScript** — ES6+, async/await, closures, prototypes
- **TypeScript** — Types, interfaces, generics
- **React.js** — Components, hooks, state management, routing

Resources:

- React docs
- TypeScript Handbook
- Scrimba

Projects:

- Todo app with React
- Weather dashboard
- E-commerce product page

### Phase 3: Tools & Technologies (1-2 months)

- **Next.js** — SSR, SSG, API routes
- **Tailwind CSS** — Utility-first styling
- **Testing** — Jest, React Testing Library, Cypress

Resources:

- Next.js docs
- Testing JavaScript (Kent C. Dodds)
- Tailwind docs

Projects:

- Full-stack blog with Next.js
- Component library
- Dashboard with charts

### Phase 4: Projects (2-3 months)

- **Portfolio Projects** — 3-5 polished projects showcasing skills
- **Open Source** — Contribute to React ecosystem projects
- **Real Client Work** — Freelance or volunteer for experience

Resources:

- GitHub
- Dev.to
- Frontend Mentor

Projects:

- Social media dashboard clone
- Real-time chat app
- Animated portfolio site

### Phase 5: Job Preparation (1-2 months)

- **DSA Basics** — Arrays, strings, common patterns
- **System Design** — Frontend architecture, performance
- **Interview Prep** — Behavioral + technical questions

Resources:

- LeetCode
- Glassdoor
- Pramp

Projects:

- Polish GitHub profile
- Deploy all projects
- Practice mock interviews

## Reality check

Frontend changes fast. You'll constantly learn new frameworks and tools. CSS can be frustrating. But the creative satisfaction is unmatched.

## What a Frontend Developer actually does day to day

Frontend developers bring designs to life. You'll build the visual and interactive parts of websites and apps that users directly interact with. In practice the week looks less like continuous coding and more like a mix of building, reviewing, debugging and deciding. A typical day includes a short stand-up, two to four hours of focused build time, code review for teammates, and at least one conversation about scope or trade-offs. The people who progress fastest in this role are the ones who treat those conversations as part of the job rather than as an interruption to it.

- **Morning:** triage anything that broke overnight, then take the highest-leverage task rather than the easiest one.
- **Core hours:** deep work on the current increment — HTML/CSS, JavaScript and React/Vue/Angular are the tools you will touch most.
- **Reviews:** reading other people's changes is the fastest way to learn a codebase and the fastest way to build trust.
- **Documentation:** a short written note about why a decision was made saves hours for the next person, often you in three months.
- **Learning:** the field moves; an hour a week on fundamentals beats a weekend binge every quarter.

## Is Frontend Developer the right fit for you?

This path suits you if several of the following are true. It is worth being honest here — switching after six months costs far more than choosing carefully now.

- You have a strong eye for design and aesthetics
- You enjoy seeing immediate visual results from your work
- You're creative and detail-oriented
- You love making things look and feel amazing

> **Honest difficulty:** Frontend changes fast. You'll constantly learn new frameworks and tools. CSS can be frustrating. But the creative satisfaction is unmatched. Competition is rated high and the entry barrier low, with realistic time to job-ready around 6-12 months (basics) → 2-3 years (expert).

## Frontend Developer salary in 2027

Compensation for frontend developers reflects scope more than years served. Excellent — every company needs frontend developers. Growing demand for React/Next.js specialists. The bands below are annual gross figures; product companies pay above them, services and agency employers below.

Frontend Developer salary bands, 2027

| Level | Experience | India | Global (USD) | What the role owns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Entry / junior | 0–2 years | ₹4-15 LPA (entry) | $50K-80K (entry) | Well-scoped tasks with close review |
| Mid-level | 3–5 years | Between the entry and senior bands | Between the entry and senior bands | Owns features end to end, mentors juniors |
| Senior | 6+ years | ₹15-40 LPA (senior) | $120K-200K+ (senior) | Owns systems, sets technical direction |
| Lead / staff | 9+ years | Above the senior band, plus equity at product companies | Above the senior band, plus equity | Leverage through other engineers and architecture |

Three factors move you up these bands faster than time does: specialising in one high-demand area rather than staying general, owning a system end to end so you can describe impact in numbers, and changing employer at the right moment — external moves still outpace internal raises in most markets. Use the [salary predictor](https://www.skillta.tech/salary-predictor) to check the band for your specific city and experience level.

## The complete Frontend Developer skill map

You need 7 core competencies to be credible in interviews for this role. The table maps each one to why employers care and how it gets tested, so you can prioritise instead of trying to learn everything at once.

Core Frontend Developer skills and how they are assessed

| Skill | Why it matters | How interviewers test it | Time to proficiency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HTML/CSS | Most common source of production incidents when done badly | Live coding exercise | 3–5 months |
| JavaScript | Most common source of production incidents when done badly | Whiteboard or design discussion | 2–4 weeks |
| React/Vue/Angular | Foundation that every later topic depends on | Live coding exercise | 4–8 weeks |
| TypeScript | What separates a mid-level candidate from a junior one | Live coding exercise | 2–3 months |
| Responsive Design | What separates a mid-level candidate from a junior one | Debugging a broken example | 2–3 months |
| Git | Most common source of production incidents when done badly | Debugging a broken example | 4–8 weeks |
| UI/UX Principles | Most common source of production incidents when done badly | Take-home review and follow-up questions | 4–8 weeks |

## Week-by-week Frontend Developer learning plan

The roadmap phases above tell you what to learn. This plan tells you when, assuming 10–15 hours a week of focused study. Slipping a week is normal; skipping the build column is not — the projects are what make the learning stick and what fills your portfolio.

Week-by-week Frontend Developer study plan (10–15 hours a week)

| Timeline | Phase | What to learn | What to build that week |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Weeks 1–2 | Phase 1: Fundamentals | HTML5 — Semantic markup, accessibility, forms | Personal portfolio website |
| Weeks 3–4 | Phase 1: Fundamentals | CSS3 — Flexbox, Grid, animations, responsive design | Responsive landing page |
| Weeks 5–6 | Phase 1: Fundamentals | JavaScript Basics — Variables, functions, DOM manipulation, events | Interactive form |
| Weeks 7–8 | Phase 2: Core Skills | Advanced JavaScript — ES6+, async/await, closures, prototypes | Todo app with React |
| Weeks 9–10 | Phase 2: Core Skills | TypeScript — Types, interfaces, generics | Weather dashboard |
| Weeks 11–12 | Phase 2: Core Skills | React.js — Components, hooks, state management, routing | E-commerce product page |
| Weeks 13–14 | Phase 3: Tools & Technologies | Next.js — SSR, SSG, API routes | Full-stack blog with Next.js |
| Weeks 15–16 | Phase 3: Tools & Technologies | Tailwind CSS — Utility-first styling | Component library |
| Weeks 17–18 | Phase 3: Tools & Technologies | Testing — Jest, React Testing Library, Cypress | Dashboard with charts |
| Weeks 19–20 | Phase 4: Projects | Portfolio Projects — 3-5 polished projects showcasing skills | Social media dashboard clone |
| Weeks 21–22 | Phase 4: Projects | Open Source — Contribute to React ecosystem projects | Real-time chat app |
| Weeks 23–24 | Phase 4: Projects | Real Client Work — Freelance or volunteer for experience | Animated portfolio site |
| Weeks 25–26 | Phase 5: Job Preparation | DSA Basics — Arrays, strings, common patterns | Polish GitHub profile |
| Weeks 27–28 | Phase 5: Job Preparation | System Design — Frontend architecture, performance | Deploy all projects |
| Weeks 29–30 | Phase 5: Job Preparation | Interview Prep — Behavioral + technical questions | Practice mock interviews |

## Portfolio projects that get interviews

Recruiters skim portfolios in under a minute, so two strong projects beat six weak ones. Each project below should be deployed, documented with a short README explaining the problem and the trade-offs, and something you can talk through for ten minutes without notes.

1. Personal portfolio website
2. Responsive landing page
3. Interactive form
4. Todo app with React
5. Weather dashboard
6. E-commerce product page
7. Full-stack blog with Next.js
8. Component library
9. Dashboard with charts
10. Social media dashboard clone

Make at least one project unmistakably yours — solve a problem you actually have, use real data, and write up what broke. Interviewers ask far better questions about original work than about a cloned tutorial app, and those questions are the ones you will answer best.

## Free resources worth using

- MDN Web Docs
- freeCodeCamp
- The Odin Project
- React docs
- TypeScript Handbook
- Scrimba
- Next.js docs
- Testing JavaScript (Kent C. Dodds)
- Tailwind docs
- GitHub
- Dev.to
- Frontend Mentor
- LeetCode
- Glassdoor
- Pramp

Pick one primary resource and one reference. Rotating between five courses feels productive and teaches very little; finishing one and building alongside it teaches a lot. Official documentation should become your default reference within the first two months.

## Frontend Developer interview preparation

Interview loops for this role typically run four to six stages. Expect a recruiter screen, a technical screen on fundamentals, a practical exercise or take-home, a deep-dive on your own projects, and a hiring-manager conversation about ownership and collaboration.

| Round | What is tested | Preparation that works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Screening | Motivation, communication, salary alignment | A 90-second summary of your work and a researched range |
| Technical fundamentals | HTML/CSS, JavaScript and React/Vue/Angular | Daily reps for four weeks, explained out loud |
| Practical exercise | Code quality, tests, judgement about scope | Timebox it and document what you deliberately left out |
| Project deep-dive | Whether you actually built what your CV claims | Be able to justify every architectural choice you made |
| Hiring manager | Ownership, conflict, how you handle being wrong | Six STAR stories including one genuine failure |

- **TypeScript:** explain how you would debug a problem involving typescript in production.
- **Responsive Design:** explain how you would debug a problem involving responsive design in production.
- **Git:** walk through a trade-off you made using git and what you would do differently.
- **UI/UX Principles:** walk through a trade-off you made using ui/ux principles and what you would do differently.
- **HTML/CSS:** describe how html/css fits into the systems you have built.
- **JavaScript:** compare two approaches within javascript and justify your default choice.
- **React/Vue/Angular:** describe how react/vue/angular fits into the systems you have built.

## Career progression and where this path leads

| Stage | Typical years | Scope | Common next step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Junior | 0–2 | Well-defined tasks, close review | Own a full feature without supervision |
| Mid-level | 3–5 | Features end to end, some mentoring | Own a service or subsystem |
| Senior | 6–9 | Systems, technical direction, cross-team work | Staff engineer or engineering manager |
| Lead / staff / manager | 10+ | Organisational leverage, architecture, hiring | Principal engineer, head of engineering, or founder |

Lateral moves are common and healthy from this role. Frontend Developer experience transfers well into adjacent specialisations, product engineering, and technical leadership. Use [compare careers](https://www.skillta.tech/compare) to see how the salary, difficulty and demand of two paths stack up before committing.

## Mistakes that slow people down

1. Collecting tutorials instead of finishing projects. Completion is the skill being trained.
2. Learning adjacent tools before the core ones. Get HTML/CSS and JavaScript solid first.
3. Building only what the tutorial shows. The learning happens when something breaks and nobody has written the fix down.
4. Waiting until you feel ready to apply. Interview practice is a skill and it is trained by interviewing.
5. No public trail. A deployed link and a written case study is worth more than a private repository.
6. Ignoring fundamentals because the stack is modern. Complexity, data modelling and debugging are still what interviews test.

## Frontend Developer — frequently asked questions

### How long does it take to become a frontend developer?

6-12 months to job-ready for someone starting from scratch and studying 10–15 hours a week. People coming from an adjacent technical role usually move faster because they already understand how teams ship software.

### Is Frontend Developer a good career in 2027?

Demand is rated very high. Excellent — every company needs frontend developers. Growing demand for React/Next.js specialists.

### Do I need a degree to become a frontend developer?

No, though it still helps for visa-sponsored roles and large enterprises. What replaces it is evidence: deployed projects, a public code history, and the ability to explain your decisions clearly.

### How hard is it really?

Difficulty is moderate — roughly 3 out of 10. Frontend changes fast. You'll constantly learn new frameworks and tools. CSS can be frustrating. But the creative satisfaction is unmatched.

### What should I learn first?

Start with Fundamentals — specifically HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript Basics. Everything later in the roadmap assumes this foundation.

### Can I switch to Frontend Developer from a non-technical background?

Yes, and thousands do each year. The realistic timeline is 6-12 months (basics) → 2-3 years (expert), the main risk is quitting in month four, and the strongest mitigation is a public build streak plus one person who expects progress from you weekly.

### Will AI replace frontend developers?

AI has changed the work rather than removed it. Code generation raised the floor, and the value moved toward design, debugging, evaluating correctness and understanding systems — the parts current models handle least reliably.

> **Next step:** Not certain this is your best fit? The [free career quiz](https://www.skillta.tech/quiz) takes five minutes, or run the [skill gap analyzer](https://www.skillta.tech/skill-gap-analyzer) to see exactly what stands between you and a frontend developer role.

# Backend Developer Roadmap

> Build the engines that power applications

Canonical: https://www.skillta.tech/roadmaps/backend-developer

Backend developers create the server-side logic, databases, and APIs that make applications work. You're the architect behind the scenes.

## Key facts

| Metric | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Difficulty | Hard |
| Time to job-ready | 8-14 months to job-ready |
| Demand | Very High |
| Salary (India) | ₹5-18 LPA (entry) → ₹20-50 LPA (senior) |
| Salary (Global) | $60K-90K (entry) → $130K-220K+ (senior) |
| Growth | Excellent — backend skills are foundational and always in demand. |

## Required skills

- Node.js/Python/Java
- Databases (SQL/NoSQL)
- REST APIs
- Authentication
- Cloud Services
- Docker
- System Design

## Learning roadmap

### Phase 1: Fundamentals (2-3 months)

- **Programming Language** — Python, Node.js, or Java — pick one and master it
- **Data Structures & Algorithms** — Arrays, trees, graphs, sorting, searching
- **Computer Science Basics** — OS, networking, HTTP protocol

Resources:

- CS50 (Harvard)
- freeCodeCamp
- NeetCode

Projects:

- CLI task manager
- Basic calculator
- File organizer script

### Phase 2: Core Skills (2-3 months)

- **Databases** — PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis — querying, indexing, optimization
- **REST API Design** — CRUD operations, authentication, error handling
- **Version Control** — Git workflows, branching strategies

Resources:

- PostgreSQL docs
- MongoDB University
- REST API Tutorial

Projects:

- Blog API with authentication
- URL shortener
- Inventory management API

### Phase 3: Tools & Technologies (2-3 months)

- **Docker & Containers** — Containerization, Docker Compose
- **Cloud Services** — AWS/GCP basics, deployment, S3, Lambda
- **Message Queues** — RabbitMQ, Redis pub/sub, event-driven design

Resources:

- Docker docs
- AWS Free Tier
- Fireship.io

Projects:

- Microservices architecture
- Serverless API
- Real-time notification system

### Phase 4: Projects (2-3 months)

- **Full-Stack App** — Build end-to-end with a frontend
- **System Design** — Design scalable architectures
- **Open Source** — Contribute to backend frameworks

Resources:

- System Design Primer
- GitHub
- Dev.to

Projects:

- E-commerce platform
- Real-time chat system
- Payment integration

### Phase 5: Job Preparation (1-2 months)

- **DSA Practice** — LeetCode medium/hard problems
- **System Design Interviews** — Practice designing scalable systems
- **Behavioral Prep** — STAR method, past experiences

Resources:

- LeetCode
- Grokking System Design
- Pramp

Projects:

- Polish portfolio
- Write technical blog posts
- Mock interviews

## Reality check

Backend is less glamorous — no one sees your work. Debugging production issues at 2 AM happens. But the pay is great and the skills transfer across industries.

## What a Backend Developer actually does day to day

Backend developers create the server-side logic, databases, and APIs that make applications work. You're the architect behind the scenes. In practice the week looks less like continuous coding and more like a mix of building, reviewing, debugging and deciding. A typical day includes a short stand-up, two to four hours of focused build time, code review for teammates, and at least one conversation about scope or trade-offs. The people who progress fastest in this role are the ones who treat those conversations as part of the job rather than as an interruption to it.

- **Morning:** triage anything that broke overnight, then take the highest-leverage task rather than the easiest one.
- **Core hours:** deep work on the current increment — Node.js/Python/Java, Databases (SQL/NoSQL) and REST APIs are the tools you will touch most.
- **Reviews:** reading other people's changes is the fastest way to learn a codebase and the fastest way to build trust.
- **Documentation:** a short written note about why a decision was made saves hours for the next person, often you in three months.
- **Learning:** the field moves; an hour a week on fundamentals beats a weekend binge every quarter.

## Is Backend Developer the right fit for you?

This path suits you if several of the following are true. It is worth being honest here — switching after six months costs far more than choosing carefully now.

- You love logical thinking and system design
- You prefer working with data and algorithms over visuals
- You enjoy solving complex architectural problems
- You want to understand how systems scale

> **Honest difficulty:** Backend is less glamorous — no one sees your work. Debugging production issues at 2 AM happens. But the pay is great and the skills transfer across industries. Competition is rated medium and the entry barrier medium, with realistic time to job-ready around 8-14 months (basics) → 3-4 years (expert).

## Backend Developer salary in 2027

Compensation for backend developers reflects scope more than years served. Excellent — backend skills are foundational and always in demand. The bands below are annual gross figures; product companies pay above them, services and agency employers below.

Backend Developer salary bands, 2027

| Level | Experience | India | Global (USD) | What the role owns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Entry / junior | 0–2 years | ₹5-18 LPA (entry) | $60K-90K (entry) | Well-scoped tasks with close review |
| Mid-level | 3–5 years | Between the entry and senior bands | Between the entry and senior bands | Owns features end to end, mentors juniors |
| Senior | 6+ years | ₹20-50 LPA (senior) | $130K-220K+ (senior) | Owns systems, sets technical direction |

4. Waiting until you feel ready to apply. Interview practice is a skill and it is trained by interviewing.
5. No public trail. A deployed link and a written case study is worth more than a private repository.
6. Ignoring fundamentals because the stack is modern. Complexity, data modelling and debugging are still what interviews test.

## Backend Developer — frequently asked questions

### How long does it take to become a backend developer?

8-14 months to job-ready for someone starting from scratch and studying 15–20 hours a week. People coming from an adjacent technical role usually move faster because they already understand how teams ship software.

### Is Backend Developer a good career in 2027?

Demand is rated very high. Excellent — backend skills are foundational and always in demand.

### Do I need a degree to become a backend developer?

No, though it still helps for visa-sponsored roles and large enterprises. What replaces it is evidence: deployed projects, a public code history, and the ability to explain your decisions clearly.

### How hard is it really?

Difficulty is hard — roughly 4 out of 10. Backend is less glamorous — no one sees your work. Debugging production issues at 2 AM happens. But the pay is great and the skills transfer across industries.

### What should I learn first?

Start with Fundamentals — specifically Programming Language, Data Structures & Algorithms and Computer Science Basics. Everything later in the roadmap assumes this foundation.

### Can I switch to Backend Developer from a non-technical background?

Yes, and thousands do each year. The realistic timeline is 8-14 months (basics) → 3-4 years (expert), the main risk is quitting in month four, and the strongest mitigation is a public build streak plus one person who expects progress from you weekly.

### Will AI replace backend developers?

AI has changed the work rather than removed it. Code generation raised the floor, and the value moved toward design, debugging, evaluating correctness and understanding systems — the parts current models handle least reliably.

> **Next step:** Not certain this is your best fit? The [free career quiz](https://www.skillta.tech/quiz) takes five minutes, or run the [skill gap analyzer](https://www.skillta.tech/skill-gap-analyzer) to see exactly what stands between you and a backend developer role.

- [Blog](https://www.skillta.tech/blog)

# Data Scientist Roadmap

> Turn data into actionable intelligence

Canonical: https://www.skillta.tech/roadmaps/data-scientist

Data scientists analyze complex datasets to find patterns, build predictive models, and drive business decisions with data-driven insights.

## Key facts

| Metric | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Difficulty | Very Hard |
| Time to job-ready | 12-18 months to job-ready |
| Demand | Very High |
| Salary (India) | ₹6-20 LPA (entry) → ₹25-60 LPA (senior) |
| Salary (Global) | $70K-100K (entry) → $150K-250K+ (senior) |
| Growth | Outstanding — AI/ML boom is creating massive demand. One of the highest-paid tech careers. |

## Required skills

- Python/R
- Statistics
- Machine Learning
- SQL
- Data Visualization
- Pandas/NumPy
- Communication

## Learning roadmap

### Phase 1: Fundamentals (2-3 months)

- **Python Programming** — Master Python for data work
- **Mathematics** — Linear algebra, calculus, probability
- **Statistics** — Hypothesis testing, distributions, regression

Resources:

- Khan Academy
- 3Blue1Brown
- Python for Data Analysis (book)

Projects:

- Statistical analysis of a dataset
- Data cleaning pipeline
- Exploratory data analysis

### Phase 2: Core Skills (3-4 months)

- **Pandas & NumPy** — Data manipulation and numerical computing
- **Data Visualization** — Matplotlib, Seaborn, Plotly
- **SQL** — Complex queries, joins, window functions

Resources:

- Kaggle Learn
- Mode Analytics SQL Tutorial
- DataCamp

Projects:

- Sales analysis dashboard
- Customer segmentation
- A/B test analysis

### Phase 3: Machine Learning (3-4 months)

- **Supervised Learning** — Regression, classification, ensemble methods
- **Unsupervised Learning** — Clustering, PCA, anomaly detection
- **Deep Learning Basics** — Neural networks, TensorFlow/PyTorch intro

Resources:

- Andrew Ng's ML Course
- fast.ai
- Scikit-learn docs

Projects:

- House price prediction
- Image classifier
- Recommendation engine

### Phase 4: Projects & Portfolio (2-3 months)

- **End-to-End Projects** — From data collection to deployment
- **Kaggle Competitions** — Compete and learn from others
- **Blog Writing** — Document your findings and process

Resources:

- Kaggle
- Towards Data Science
- GitHub

Projects:

- NLP sentiment analyzer
- Time series forecasting
- ML-powered web app

### Phase 5: Job Preparation (1-2 months)

- **Case Studies** — Practice business case interviews
- **Technical Interviews** — ML concepts, coding, statistics
- **Portfolio Polish** — GitHub, blog, Kaggle profile

Resources:

- Glassdoor
- Interview Query
- Ace the Data Science Interview (book)

Projects:

- Create portfolio website
- Record project walkthroughs
- Mock interviews

## Reality check

80% of the job is cleaning data, not building cool models. Math is non-negotiable. The field is overhyped for beginners but genuinely rewarding for those who persist.

## What a Data Scientist actually does day to day

Data scientists analyze complex datasets to find patterns, build predictive models, and drive business decisions with data-driven insights. In practice the week looks less like continuous coding and more like a mix of building, reviewing, debugging and deciding. A typical day includes a short stand-up, two to four hours of focused build time, code review for teammates, and at least one conversation about scope or trade-offs. The people who progress fastest in this role are the ones who treat those conversations as part of the job rather than as an interruption to it.

- **Morning:** triage anything that broke overnight, then take the highest-leverage task rather than the easiest one.
- **Core hours:** deep work on the current increment — Python/R, Statistics and Machine Learning are the tools you will touch most.
- **Reviews:** reading other people's changes is the fastest way to learn a codebase and the fastest way to build trust.
- **Documentation:** a short written note about why a decision was made saves hours for the next person, often you in three months.
- **Learning:** the field moves; an hour a week on fundamentals beats a weekend binge every quarter.

## Is Data Scientist the right fit for you?

This path suits you if several of the following are true. It is worth being honest here — switching after six months costs far more than choosing carefully now.

- You love mathematics and statistics
- You're curious about finding hidden patterns
- You enjoy working with large datasets
- You want to make decisions based on evidence

> **Honest difficulty:** 80% of the job is cleaning data, not building cool models. Math is non-negotiable. The field is overhyped for beginners but genuinely rewarding for those who persist. Competition is rated very high and the entry barrier high, with realistic time to job-ready around 12-18 months (basics) → 3-5 years (expert).

## Data Scientist salary in 2027

Compensation for data scientists reflects scope more than years served. Outstanding — AI/ML boom is creating massive demand. One of the highest-paid tech careers. The bands below are annual gross figures; product companies pay above them, services and agency employers below.

Data Scientist salary bands, 2027

| Level | Experience | India | Global (USD) | What the role owns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Entry / junior | 0–2 years | ₹6-20 LPA (entry) | $70K-100K (entry) | Well-scoped tasks with close review |
| Mid-level | 3–5 years | Between the entry and senior bands | Between the entry and senior bands | Owns features end to end, mentors juniors |
| Senior | 6+ years | ₹25-60 LPA (senior) | $150K-250K+ (senior) | Owns systems, sets technical direction |
| Lead / staff | 9+ years | Above the senior band, plus equity at product companies | Above the senior band, plus equity | Leverage through other engineers and architecture |

Three factors move you up these bands faster than time does: specialising in one high-demand area rather than staying general, owning a system end to end so you can describe impact in numbers, and changing employer at the right moment — external moves still outpace internal raises in most markets. Use the [salary predictor](https://www.skillta.tech/salary-predictor) to check the band for your specific city and experience level.

## The complete Data Scientist skill map

You need 7 core competencies to be credible in interviews for this role. The table maps each one to why employers care and how it gets tested, so you can prioritise instead of trying to learn everything at once.

Core Data Scientist skills and how they are assessed

| Skill | Why it matters | How interviewers test it | Time to proficiency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Python/R | Appears in the majority of job descriptions for this role | Deep questions about a project on your CV | 3–5 months |
| Statistics | What separates a mid-level candidate from a junior one | Debugging a broken example | 2–4 weeks |
| Machine Learning | The difference between shipping and shipping something maintainable | Deep questions about a project on your CV | 4–8 weeks |
| SQL | Most common source of production incidents when done badly | Deep questions about a project on your CV | 3–5 months |
| Data Visualization | Appears in the majority of job descriptions for this role | Live coding exercise | 2–4 weeks |
| Pandas/NumPy | Foundation that every later topic depends on | Whiteboard or design discussion | 2–4 weeks |
| Communication | Appears in the majority of job descriptions for this role | Debugging a broken example | 2–4 weeks |

## Week-by-week Data Scientist learning plan

The roadmap phases above tell you what to learn. This plan tells you when, assuming 20+ hours a week of focused study. Slipping a week is normal; skipping the build column is not — the projects are what make the learning stick and what fills your portfolio.

Week-by-week Data Scientist study plan (20+ hours a week)

| Timeline | Phase | What to learn | What to build that week |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Weeks 1–2 | Phase 1: Fundamentals | Python Programming — Master Python for data work | Statistical analysis of a dataset |
| Weeks 3–4 | Phase 1: Fundamentals | Mathematics — Linear algebra, calculus, probability | Data cleaning pipeline |
| Weeks 5–6 | Phase 1: Fundamentals | Statistics — Hypothesis testing, distributions, regression | Exploratory data analysis |
| Weeks 7–8 | Phase 2: Core Skills | Pandas & NumPy — Data manipulation and numerical computing | Sales analysis dashboard |
| Weeks 9–10 | Phase 2: Core Skills | Data Visualization — Matplotlib, Seaborn, Plotly | Customer segmentation |
| Weeks 11–12 | Phase 2: Core Skills | SQL — Complex queries, joins, window functions | A/B test analysis |
| Weeks 13–14 | Phase 3: Machine Learning | Supervised Learning — Regression, classification, ensemble methods | House price prediction |
| Weeks 15–16 | Phase 3: Machine Learning | Unsupervised Learning — Clustering, PCA, anomaly detection | Image classifier |
| Weeks 17–18 | Phase 3: Machine Learning | Deep Learning Basics — Neural networks, TensorFlow/PyTorch intro | Recommendation engine |
| Weeks 19–20 | Phase 4: Projects & Portfolio | End-to-End Projects — From data collection to deployment | NLP sentiment analyzer |
| Weeks 21–22 | Phase 4: Projects & Portfolio | Kaggle Competitions — Compete and learn from others | Time series forecasting |
| Weeks 23–24 | Phase 4: Projects & Portfolio | Blog Writing — Document your findings and process | ML-powered web app |
| Weeks 25–26 | Phase 5: Job Preparation | Case Studies — Practice business case interviews | Create portfolio website |
| Weeks 27–28 | Phase 5: Job Preparation | Technical Interviews — ML concepts, coding, statistics | Record project walkthroughs |
| Weeks 29–30 | Phase 5: Job Preparation | Portfolio Polish — GitHub, blog, Kaggle profile | Mock interviews |

## Portfolio projects that get interviews

Recruiters skim portfolios in under a minute, so two strong projects beat six weak ones. Each project below should be deployed, documented with a short README explaining the problem and the trade-offs, and something you can talk through for ten minutes without notes.

1. Statistical analysis of a dataset
2. Data cleaning pipeline
3. Exploratory data analysis
4. Sales analysis dashboard
5. Customer segmentation
6. A/B test analysis
7. House price prediction
8. Image classifier
9. Recommendation engine
10. NLP sentiment analyzer

Make at least one project unmistakably yours — solve a problem you actually have, use real data, and write up what broke. Interviewers ask far better questions about original work than about a cloned tutorial app, and those questions are the ones you will answer best.

## Free resources worth using

- Khan Academy
- 3Blue1Brown
- Python for Data Analysis (book)
- Kaggle Learn
- Mode Analytics SQL Tutorial
- DataCamp
- Andrew Ng's ML Course
- fast.ai
- Scikit-learn docs
- Kaggle
- Towards Data Science
- GitHub
- Glassdoor
- Interview Query
- Ace the Data Science Interview (book)

Pick one primary resource and one reference. Rotating between five courses feels productive and teaches very little; finishing one and building alongside it teaches a lot. Official documentation should become your default reference within the first two months.

## Data Scientist interview preparation

Interview loops for this role typically run four to six stages. Expect a recruiter screen, a technical screen on fundamentals, a practical exercise or take-home, a deep-dive on your own projects, and a hiring-manager conversation about ownership and collaboration.

| Round | What is tested | Preparation that works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Screening | Motivation, communication, salary alignment | A 90-second summary of your work and a researched range |
| Technical fundamentals | Python/R, Statistics and Machine Learning | Daily reps for four weeks, explained out loud |
| Practical exercise | Code quality, tests, judgement about scope | Timebox it and document what you deliberately left out |
| Project deep-dive | Whether you actually built what your CV claims | Be able to justify every architectural choice you made |
| Hiring manager | Ownership, conflict, how you handle being wrong | Six STAR stories including one genuine failure |

- **Communication:** compare two approaches within communication and justify your default choice.
- **Python/R:** compare two approaches within python/r and justify your default choice.
- **Statistics:** describe how statistics fits into the systems you have built.
- **Machine Learning:** compare two approaches within machine learning and justify your default choice.
- **SQL:** compare two approaches within sql and justify your default choice.
- **Data Visualization:** describe how data visualization fits into the systems you have built.
- **Pandas/NumPy:** explain how you would debug a problem involving pandas/numpy in production.

## Career progression and where this path leads

| Stage | Typical years | Scope | Common next step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Junior | 0–2 | Well-defined tasks, close review | Own a full feature without supervision |
| Mid-level | 3–5 | Features end to end, some mentoring | Own a service or subsystem |
| Senior | 6–9 | Systems, technical direction, cross-team work | Staff engineer or engineering manager |
| Lead / staff / manager | 10+ | Organisational leverage, architecture, hiring | Principal engineer, head of engineering, or founder |

Lateral moves are common and healthy from this role. Data Scientist experience transfers well into adjacent specialisations, product engineering, and technical leadership. Use [compare careers](https://www.skillta.tech/compare) to see how the salary, difficulty and demand of two paths stack up before committing.

## Mistakes that slow people down

1. Collecting tutorials instead of finishing projects. Completion is the skill being trained.
2. Learning adjacent tools before the core ones. Get Python/R and Statistics solid first.
3. Building only what the tutorial shows. The learning happens when something breaks and nobody has written the fix down.
4. Waiting until you feel ready to apply. Interview practice is a skill and it is trained by interviewing.
5. No public trail. A deployed link and a written case study is worth more than a private repository.
6. Ignoring fundamentals because the stack is modern. Complexity, data modelling and debugging are still what interviews test.

No, though it still helps for visa-sponsored roles and large enterprises. What replaces it is evidence: deployed projects, a public code history, and the ability to explain your decisions clearly.

### How hard is it really?

### What should I learn first?

Start with Fundamentals — specifically Python Programming, Mathematics and Statistics. Everything later in the roadmap assumes this foundation.

Yes, and thousands do each year. The realistic timeline is 12-18 months (basics) → 3-5 years (expert), the main risk is quitting in month four, and the strongest mitigation is a public build streak plus one person who expects progress from you weekly.

# Cybersecurity Specialist Roadmap

> Protect systems and hunt vulnerabilities

Canonical: https://www.skillta.tech/roadmaps/cybersecurity-specialist

Cybersecurity specialists protect organizations from threats, find vulnerabilities, and ensure data safety in an increasingly digital world.

## Key facts

| Metric | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Difficulty | Hard |
| Time to job-ready | 10-16 months to job-ready |
| Demand | Very High |
| Salary (India) | ₹5-15 LPA (entry) → ₹20-50 LPA (senior) |
| Salary (Global) | $65K-95K (entry) → $130K-200K+ (senior) |
| Growth | Outstanding — cybersecurity talent shortage is massive globally. One of the most recession-proof tech careers. |

## Required skills

- Networking
- Linux
- Python/Bash
- Penetration Testing
- Cryptography
- SIEM Tools
- Compliance

## Learning roadmap

### Phase 1: Fundamentals (2-3 months)

- **Networking** — TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP, firewalls, VPNs
- **Linux** — Command line, file systems, permissions
- **Operating Systems** — Windows/Linux security, processes

Resources:

- CompTIA Network+
- TryHackMe
- Linux Journey

Projects:

- Set up a home lab
- Network traffic analysis
- Linux hardening

### Phase 2: Core Skills (3-4 months)

- **Security Fundamentals** — CIA triad, threat modeling, risk assessment
- **Web Application Security** — OWASP Top 10, SQL injection, XSS
- **Cryptography** — Encryption, hashing, PKI, certificates

Resources:

- OWASP
- PortSwigger Web Security Academy
- CompTIA Security+

Projects:

- Vulnerable app exploitation
- Security audit report
- Encrypted messaging tool

### Phase 3: Tools & Technologies (2-3 months)

- **Penetration Testing** — Nmap, Burp Suite, Metasploit, Wireshark
- **SIEM & Monitoring** — Splunk, ELK Stack, log analysis
- **Scripting** — Python and Bash for automation

Resources:

- Hack The Box
- SANS courses
- CyberDefenders

Projects:

- CTF challenges
- Automated vulnerability scanner
- Incident response playbook

### Phase 4: Specialization (2-3 months)

- **Choose a Path** — Pentesting, SOC analyst, cloud security, or forensics
- **Certifications** — CEH, CompTIA Security+, OSCP
- **Bug Bounties** — Practice on real targets legally

Resources:

- HackerOne
- Bugcrowd
- Offensive Security

Projects:

- Bug bounty hunting
- Security assessment report
- Malware analysis

### Phase 5: Job Preparation (1-2 months)

- **Portfolio** — Document CTFs, projects, certifications
- **Networking** — Join security communities, conferences
- **Interview Prep** — Technical scenarios, incident response

Resources:

- LinkedIn
- InfoSec conferences
- Reddit r/netsec

Projects:

- Write security blog posts
- Present at local meetups
- Mock incident response

## Career progression and where this path leads

| Stage | Typical years | Scope | Common next step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Junior | 0–2 | Well-defined tasks, close review | Own a full feature without supervision |
| Mid-level | 3–5 | Features end to end, some mentoring | Own a service or subsystem |
| Senior | 6–9 | Systems, technical direction, cross-team work | Staff engineer or engineering manager |
| Lead / staff / manager | 10+ | Organisational leverage, architecture, hiring | Principal engineer, head of engineering, or founder |

Lateral moves are common and healthy from this role. Cybersecurity Specialist experience transfers well into adjacent specialisations, product engineering, and technical leadership. Use [compare careers](https://www.skillta.tech/compare) to see how the salary, difficulty and demand of two paths stack up before committing.

## Mistakes that slow people down

1. Collecting tutorials instead of finishing projects. Completion is the skill being trained.
2. Learning adjacent tools before the core ones. Get Networking and Linux solid first.
3. Building only what the tutorial shows. The learning happens when something breaks and nobody has written the fix down.
4. Waiting until you feel ready to apply. Interview practice is a skill and it is trained by interviewing.
5. No public trail. A deployed link and a written case study is worth more than a private repository.
6. Ignoring fundamentals because the stack is modern. Complexity, data modelling and debugging are still what interviews test.

## Cybersecurity Specialist — frequently asked questions

### How long does it take to become a cybersecurity specialist?

10-16 months to job-ready for someone starting from scratch and studying 15–20 hours a week. People coming from an adjacent technical role usually move faster because they already understand how teams ship software.

### Is Cybersecurity Specialist a good career in 2027?

Demand is rated very high. Outstanding — cybersecurity talent shortage is massive globally. One of the most recession-proof tech careers.

### Do I need a degree to become a cybersecurity specialist?

No, though it still helps for visa-sponsored roles and large enterprises. What replaces it is evidence: deployed projects, a public code history, and the ability to explain your decisions clearly.

### How hard is it really?

Difficulty is hard — roughly 4 out of 10. It's not like the movies. Lots of compliance work, log analysis, and documentation. But the ethical hacking side is genuinely exciting and the job security is unmatched.

### What should I learn first?

Start with Fundamentals — specifically Networking, Linux and Operating Systems. Everything later in the roadmap assumes this foundation.

### Can I switch to Cybersecurity Specialist from a non-technical background?

Yes, and thousands do each year. The realistic timeline is 10-16 months (entry) → 3-5 years (expert), the main risk is quitting in month four, and the strongest mitigation is a public build streak plus one person who expects progress from you weekly.

### Will AI replace cybersecurity specialists?

AI has changed the work rather than removed it. Code generation raised the floor, and the value moved toward design, debugging, evaluating correctness and understanding systems — the parts current models handle least reliably.

> **Next step:** Not certain this is your best fit? The [free career quiz](https://www.skillta.tech/quiz) takes five minutes, or run the [skill gap analyzer](https://www.skillta.tech/skill-gap-analyzer) to see exactly what stands between you and a cybersecurity specialist role.

# UI/UX Designer Roadmap

> Design experiences people love to use

Canonical: https://www.skillta.tech/roadmaps/uiux-designer

UI/UX designers research user needs, create wireframes and prototypes, and design intuitive interfaces that solve real problems beautifully.

## Key facts

| Metric | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Difficulty | Moderate |
| Time to job-ready | 6-10 months to job-ready |
| Demand | High |
| Salary (India) | ₹4-12 LPA (entry) → ₹15-35 LPA (senior) |
| Salary (Global) | $55K-80K (entry) → $110K-180K+ (senior) |
| Growth | Strong — companies increasingly value design. Product design roles are expanding rapidly. |

## Required skills

- Figma/Sketch
- User Research
- Wireframing
- Prototyping
- Design Systems
- Typography
- Usability Testing

## Learning roadmap

### Phase 1: Fundamentals (1-2 months)

- **Design Principles** — Color theory, typography, layout, hierarchy
- **UX Fundamentals** — User-centered design, information architecture
- **Figma Basics** — Tools, components, auto-layout

Resources:

- Google UX Design Certificate
- Refactoring UI
- Figma tutorials

Projects:

- Redesign a bad website
- Mobile app wireframes
- Style guide creation

### Phase 2: Core Skills (2-3 months)

- **User Research** — Interviews, surveys, personas, journey maps
- **Wireframing & Prototyping** — Low-fi to high-fi, interactive prototypes
- **Design Systems** — Component libraries, tokens, documentation

Resources:

- Nielsen Norman Group
- Interaction Design Foundation
- Laws of UX

Projects:

- User research case study
- Design system from scratch
- Prototype a fintech app

### Phase 3: Advanced Design (2-3 months)

- **Motion Design** — Micro-interactions, transitions, animation principles
- **Accessibility** — WCAG guidelines, inclusive design
- **Frontend Basics** — HTML/CSS awareness for better handoff

Resources:

- Material Design
- Apple HIG
- A11y Project

Projects:

- Accessible design audit
- Animated prototype
- Design-to-code handoff

### Phase 4: Portfolio (2-3 months)

- **Case Studies** — 3-5 detailed case studies with process
- **Portfolio Website** — Beautiful, showcasing your best work
- **Real Projects** — Freelance, volunteer, or redesign challenges

Resources:

- Behance
- Dribbble
- UX Collective

Projects:

- End-to-end app design
- Website redesign case study
- Design sprint exercise

### Phase 5: Job Preparation (1 month)

- **Design Challenges** — Whiteboard exercises, take-home assignments
- **Portfolio Reviews** — Get feedback from senior designers
- **Interview Prep** — Present case studies confidently

Resources:

- ADPList (mentorship)
- Glassdoor
- Design communities

Projects:

- Timed design challenges
- Presentation practice
- Networking

## Reality check

You'll hear 'make the logo bigger' more than you'd like. Stakeholder management is 50% of the job. But designing something people genuinely love to use is incredibly fulfilling.

## What a UI/UX Designer actually does day to day

UI/UX designers research user needs, create wireframes and prototypes, and design intuitive interfaces that solve real problems beautifully. In practice the week looks less like continuous coding and more like a mix of building, reviewing, debugging and deciding. A typical day includes a short stand-up, two to four hours of focused build time, code review for teammates, and at least one conversation about scope or trade-offs. The people who progress fastest in this role are the ones who treat those conversations as part of the job rather than as an interruption to it.

- **Morning:** triage anything that broke overnight, then take the highest-leverage task rather than the easiest one.
- **Core hours:** deep work on the current increment — Figma/Sketch, User Research and Wireframing are the tools you will touch most.
- **Reviews:** reading other people's changes is the fastest way to learn a codebase and the fastest way to build trust.
- **Documentation:** a short written note about why a decision was made saves hours for the next person, often you in three months.
- **Learning:** the field moves; an hour a week on fundamentals beats a weekend binge every quarter.

## Is UI/UX Designer the right fit for you?

This path suits you if several of the following are true. It is worth being honest here — switching after six months costs far more than choosing carefully now.

- You're highly creative and visual
- You empathize with users and their frustrations
- You love both aesthetics and problem-solving
- You enjoy research and understanding human behavior

> **Honest difficulty:** You'll hear 'make the logo bigger' more than you'd like. Stakeholder management is 50% of the job. But designing something people genuinely love to use is incredibly fulfilling. Competition is rated high and the entry barrier low, with realistic time to job-ready around 6-10 months (basics) → 2-3 years (expert).

## UI/UX Designer salary in 2027

Compensation for ui/ux designers reflects scope more than years served. Strong — companies increasingly value design. Product design roles are expanding rapidly. The bands below are annual gross figures; product companies pay above them, services and agency employers below.

UI/UX Designer salary bands, 2027

| Level | Experience | India | Global (USD) | What the role owns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Entry / junior | 0–2 years | ₹4-12 LPA (entry) | $55K-80K (entry) | Well-scoped tasks with close review |
| Mid-level | 3–5 years | Between the entry and senior bands | Between the entry and senior bands | Owns features end to end, mentors juniors |
| Senior | 6+ years | ₹15-35 LPA (senior) | $110K-180K+ (senior) | Owns systems, sets technical direction |
| Lead / staff | 9+ years | Above the senior band, plus equity at product companies | Above the senior band, plus equity | Leverage through other engineers and architecture |

Three factors move you up these bands faster than time does: specialising in one high-demand area rather than staying general, owning a system end to end so you can describe impact in numbers, and changing employer at the right moment — external moves still outpace internal raises in most markets. Use the [salary predictor](https://www.skillta.tech/salary-predictor) to check the band for your specific city and experience level.

## The complete UI/UX Designer skill map

You need 7 core competencies to be credible in interviews for this role. The table maps each one to why employers care and how it gets tested, so you can prioritise instead of trying to learn everything at once.

Core UI/UX Designer skills and how they are assessed

| Skill | Why it matters | How interviewers test it | Time to proficiency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Figma/Sketch | Foundation that every later topic depends on | Take-home review and follow-up questions | 4–8 weeks |
| User Research | What separates a mid-level candidate from a junior one | Whiteboard or design discussion | 3–5 months |
| Wireframing | Appears in the majority of job descriptions for this role | Debugging a broken example | 3–5 months |
| Prototyping | The difference between shipping and shipping something maintainable | Live coding exercise | 2–4 weeks |
| Design Systems | Appears in the majority of job descriptions for this role | Live coding exercise | 2–3 months |
| Typography | Foundation that every later topic depends on | Take-home review and follow-up questions | 2–3 months |
| Usability Testing | The difference between shipping and shipping something maintainable | Deep questions about a project on your CV | 2–4 weeks |

## Week-by-week UI/UX Designer learning plan

The roadmap phases above tell you what to learn. This plan tells you when, assuming 10–15 hours a week of focused study. Slipping a week is normal; skipping the build column is not — the projects are what make the learning stick and what fills your portfolio.

Week-by-week UI/UX Designer study plan (10–15 hours a week)

| Timeline | Phase | What to learn | What to build that week |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Weeks 1–2 | Phase 1: Fundamentals | Design Principles — Color theory, typography, layout, hierarchy | Redesign a bad website |
| Weeks 3–4 | Phase 1: Fundamentals | UX Fundamentals — User-centered design, information architecture | Mobile app wireframes |
| Weeks 5–6 | Phase 1: Fundamentals | Figma Basics — Tools, components, auto-layout | Style guide creation |
| Weeks 7–8 | Phase 2: Core Skills | User Research — Interviews, surveys, personas, journey maps | User research case study |
| Weeks 9–10 | Phase 2: Core Skills | Wireframing & Prototyping — Low-fi to high-fi, interactive prototypes | Design system from scratch |
| Weeks 11–12 | Phase 2: Core Skills | Design Systems — Component libraries, tokens, documentation | Prototype a fintech app |
| Weeks 13–14 | Phase 3: Advanced Design | Motion Design — Micro-interactions, transitions, animation principles | Accessible design audit |
| Weeks 15–16 | Phase 3: Advanced Design | Accessibility — WCAG guidelines, inclusive design | Animated prototype |
| Weeks 17–18 | Phase 3: Advanced Design | Frontend Basics — HTML/CSS awareness for better handoff | Design-to-code handoff |
| Weeks 19–20 | Phase 4: Portfolio | Case Studies — 3-5 detailed case studies with process | End-to-end app design |
| Weeks 21–22 | Phase 4: Portfolio | Portfolio Website — Beautiful, showcasing your best work | Website redesign case study |
| Weeks 23–24 | Phase 4: Portfolio | Real Projects — Freelance, volunteer, or redesign challenges | Design sprint exercise |
| Weeks 25–26 | Phase 5: Job Preparation | Design Challenges — Whiteboard exercises, take-home assignments | Timed design challenges |
| Weeks 27–28 | Phase 5: Job Preparation | Portfolio Reviews — Get feedback from senior designers | Presentation practice |
| Weeks 29–30 | Phase 5: Job Preparation | Interview Prep — Present case studies confidently | Networking |

## Portfolio projects that get interviews

Recruiters skim portfolios in under a minute, so two strong projects beat six weak ones. Each project below should be deployed, documented with a short README explaining the problem and the trade-offs, and something you can talk through for ten minutes without notes.

1. Redesign a bad website
2. Mobile app wireframes
3. Style guide creation
4. User research case study
5. Design system from scratch
6. Prototype a fintech app
7. Accessible design audit
8. Animated prototype
9. Design-to-code handoff
10. End-to-end app design

Make at least one project unmistakably yours — solve a problem you actually have, use real data, and write up what broke. Interviewers ask far better questions about original work than about a cloned tutorial app, and those questions are the ones you will answer best.

## Free resources worth using

- Google UX Design Certificate
- Refactoring UI
- Figma tutorials
- Nielsen Norman Group
- Interaction Design Foundation
- Laws of UX
- Material Design
- Apple HIG
- A11y Project
- Behance
- Dribbble
- UX Collective
- ADPList (mentorship)
- Glassdoor
- Design communities

Pick one primary resource and one reference. Rotating between five courses feels productive and teaches very little; finishing one and building alongside it teaches a lot. Official documentation should become your default reference within the first two months.

## UI/UX Designer interview preparation

Interview loops for this role typically run four to six stages. Expect a recruiter screen, a technical screen on fundamentals, a practical exercise or take-home, a deep-dive on your own projects, and a hiring-manager conversation about ownership and collaboration.

| Round | What is tested | Preparation that works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Screening | Motivation, communication, salary alignment | A 90-second summary of your work and a researched range |
| Technical fundamentals | Figma/Sketch, User Research and Wireframing | Daily reps for four weeks, explained out loud |
| Practical exercise | Code quality, tests, judgement about scope | Timebox it and document what you deliberately left out |
| Project deep-dive | Whether you actually built what your CV claims | Be able to justify every architectural choice you made |
| Hiring manager | Ownership, conflict, how you handle being wrong | Six STAR stories including one genuine failure |

- **Prototyping:** describe how prototyping fits into the systems you have built.
- **Design Systems:** explain how you would debug a problem involving design systems in production.
- **Typography:** describe how typography fits into the systems you have built.
- **Usability Testing:** describe how usability testing fits into the systems you have built.
- **Figma/Sketch:** explain how you would debug a problem involving figma/sketch in production.
- **User Research:** explain how you would debug a problem involving user research in production.
- **Wireframing:** explain how you would debug a problem involving wireframing in production.

| Stage | Typical years | Scope | Common next step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Junior | 0–2 | Well-defined tasks, close review | Own a full feature without supervision |
| Mid-level | 3–5 | Features end to end, some mentoring | Own a service or subsystem |
| Senior | 6–9 | Systems, technical direction, cross-team work | Staff engineer or engineering manager |
| Lead / staff / manager | 10+ | Organisational leverage, architecture, hiring | Principal engineer, head of engineering, or founder |

Lateral moves are common and healthy from this role. UI/UX Designer experience transfers well into adjacent specialisations, product engineering, and technical leadership. Use [compare careers](https://www.skillta.tech/compare) to see how the salary, difficulty and demand of two paths stack up before committing.

# DevOps Engineer Roadmap

> Bridge development and operations seamlessly

Canonical: https://www.skillta.tech/roadmaps/devops-engineer

DevOps engineers automate deployments, manage infrastructure, and ensure applications run reliably at scale. You're the glue between code and production.

## Key facts

| Metric | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Difficulty | Hard |
| Time to job-ready | 10-14 months to job-ready |
| Demand | Very High |
| Salary (India) | ₹6-18 LPA (entry) → ₹25-55 LPA (senior) |
| Salary (Global) | $70K-100K (entry) → $140K-220K+ (senior) |
| Growth | Outstanding — cloud adoption is accelerating. DevOps/SRE roles are among the highest-paid in tech. |

## Required skills

- Linux
- Docker/Kubernetes
- CI/CD
- Cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure)
- Terraform
- Monitoring
- Scripting

## Learning roadmap

### Phase 1: Fundamentals (2-3 months)

- **Linux Administration** — Commands, scripting, networking, services
- **Networking** — TCP/IP, DNS, load balancers, firewalls
- **Scripting** — Bash and Python for automation

Resources:

- Linux Academy
- RHCSA prep
- Bash scripting guides

Projects:

- Automated backup script
- Server monitoring tool
- Network configuration

### Phase 2: Core Skills (2-3 months)

- **Docker** — Containers, images, Docker Compose, networking
- **CI/CD** — GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI
- **Version Control** — Git workflows, branching, code review

Resources:

- Docker docs
- GitHub Actions docs
- DevOps Roadmap

Projects:

- Containerize an app
- CI/CD pipeline
- Automated testing setup

### Phase 3: Cloud & Infrastructure (3-4 months)

- **Cloud Platforms** — AWS/GCP — EC2, S3, Lambda, IAM
- **Infrastructure as Code** — Terraform, CloudFormation
- **Kubernetes** — Pods, services, deployments, Helm

Resources:

- AWS Free Tier
- Terraform docs
- KodeKloud

Projects:

- Deploy app on AWS
- Terraform infrastructure
- Kubernetes cluster

### Phase 4: Monitoring & Security (2 months)

- **Monitoring** — Prometheus, Grafana, ELK Stack
- **Security** — Secret management, network policies, scanning
- **Reliability** — SLIs/SLOs, incident management, chaos engineering

Resources:

- SRE Book (Google)
- Prometheus docs
- Grafana tutorials

Projects:

- Monitoring dashboard
- Alert system
- Disaster recovery plan

### Phase 5: Job Preparation (1-2 months)

- **Certifications** — AWS SAA, CKA, Terraform Associate
- **Portfolio** — Document infrastructure projects
- **Interview Prep** — Scenario-based questions, troubleshooting

Resources:

- A Cloud Guru
- KodeKloud
- LinkedIn

Projects:

- Full production-grade deployment
- Blog about learnings
- Open source contributions

On-call rotations are real. You'll deal with production fires. The learning curve is steep but the career is incredibly stable and well-compensated.

- **Core hours:** deep work on the current increment — Linux, Docker/Kubernetes and CI/CD are the tools you will touch most.
- **Reviews:** reading other people's changes is the fastest way to learn a codebase and the fastest way to build trust.

Pick one primary resource and one reference. Rotating between five courses feels productive and teaches very little; finishing one and building alongside it teaches a lot. Official documentation should become your default reference within the first two months.

## DevOps Engineer interview preparation

Interview loops for this role typically run four to six stages. Expect a recruiter screen, a technical screen on fundamentals, a practical exercise or take-home, a deep-dive on your own projects, and a hiring-manager conversation about ownership and collaboration.

| Round | What is tested | Preparation that works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Screening | Motivation, communication, salary alignment | A 90-second summary of your work and a researched range |
| Technical fundamentals | Linux, Docker/Kubernetes and CI/CD | Daily reps for four weeks, explained out loud |
| Practical exercise | Code quality, tests, judgement about scope | Timebox it and document what you deliberately left out |
| Project deep-dive | Whether you actually built what your CV claims | Be able to justify every architectural choice you made |
| Hiring manager | Ownership, conflict, how you handle being wrong | Six STAR stories including one genuine failure |

- **Docker/Kubernetes:** explain how you would debug a problem involving docker/kubernetes in production.
- **CI/CD:** describe how ci/cd fits into the systems you have built.
- **Cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure):** walk through a trade-off you made using cloud (aws/gcp/azure) and what you would do differently.
- **Terraform:** describe how terraform fits into the systems you have built.
- **Monitoring:** compare two approaches within monitoring and justify your default choice.
- **Scripting:** compare two approaches within scripting and justify your default choice.
- **Linux:** walk through a trade-off you made using linux and what you would do differently.

## Career progression and where this path leads

| Stage | Typical years | Scope | Common next step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Junior | 0–2 | Well-defined tasks, close review | Own a full feature without supervision |
| Mid-level | 3–5 | Features end to end, some mentoring | Own a service or subsystem |
| Senior | 6–9 | Systems, technical direction, cross-team work | Staff engineer or engineering manager |
| Lead / staff / manager | 10+ | Organisational leverage, architecture, hiring | Principal engineer, head of engineering, or founder |

Lateral moves are common and healthy from this role. DevOps Engineer experience transfers well into adjacent specialisations, product engineering, and technical leadership. Use [compare careers](https://www.skillta.tech/compare) to see how the salary, difficulty and demand of two paths stack up before committing.

## Mistakes that slow people down

1. Collecting tutorials instead of finishing projects. Completion is the skill being trained.
2. Learning adjacent tools before the core ones. Get Linux and Docker/Kubernetes solid first.
3. Building only what the tutorial shows. The learning happens when something breaks and nobody has written the fix down.
4. Waiting until you feel ready to apply. Interview practice is a skill and it is trained by interviewing.
5. No public trail. A deployed link and a written case study is worth more than a private repository.
6. Ignoring fundamentals because the stack is modern. Complexity, data modelling and debugging are still what interviews test.

## DevOps Engineer — frequently asked questions

### How long does it take to become a devops engineer?

10-14 months to job-ready for someone starting from scratch and studying 15–20 hours a week. People coming from an adjacent technical role usually move faster because they already understand how teams ship software.

### Is DevOps Engineer a good career in 2027?

Demand is rated very high. Outstanding — cloud adoption is accelerating. DevOps/SRE roles are among the highest-paid in tech.

### Do I need a degree to become a devops engineer?

No, though it still helps for visa-sponsored roles and large enterprises. What replaces it is evidence: deployed projects, a public code history, and the ability to explain your decisions clearly.

### How hard is it really?

Difficulty is hard — roughly 4 out of 10. On-call rotations are real. You'll deal with production fires. The learning curve is steep but the career is incredibly stable and well-compensated.

### What should I learn first?

Start with Fundamentals — specifically Linux Administration, Networking and Scripting. Everything later in the roadmap assumes this foundation.

### Can I switch to DevOps Engineer from a non-technical background?

Yes, and thousands do each year. The realistic timeline is 10-14 months (entry) → 3-4 years (expert), the main risk is quitting in month four, and the strongest mitigation is a public build streak plus one person who expects progress from you weekly.

### Will AI replace devops engineers?

AI has changed the work rather than removed it. Code generation raised the floor, and the value moved toward design, debugging, evaluating correctness and understanding systems — the parts current models handle least reliably.
